newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian currency board may face attack - NSS.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian currency board may face attack - NSS.

text.p: Bulgaria's National Security Service (NSS) warned on Tuesday against attempts by local business conglomerates to undermine a restrictive currency board regime aimed at stabilising the economy.
"Opponents of the currency board are some big Bulgarian private business groupings connected to Bulgarian capital syphoned abroad," NSS director-in-charge Vladimir Manolov told a news conference.

The first task of the new reformist government is to introduce the currency board, prescribed by the International Monetary Fund, in July. This is a fixed exchange rate regime designed to stabilise the country's shaky banks and volatile currency.

Central bank lending to the government and commercial banks will be banned. The national currency, the lev, is pegged to an anchor currency at a fixed rate and the amount of levs in circulation must be matched precisely by the foreign exchange reserves.
Failure to implement the system would result in Bulgaria not meeting international lenders' reform targets and ensuing suspension of agreed funding programmes.

"The conglomerates oppose all attributes of the currency board, which are banned access to state money, strengthened control of bank transactions, impediments to investment of capital with dubious origin, transparancy of privatisation deals," said Manolov.

Politicians and economists attribute Bulgaria's current economic crisis to asset stripping of profitable state companies and syphoning of funds abroad by businesmen from the former Communist Party in the past seven years.
"Some of them promulgate their interests through local banks," said Manolov.

Manolov said the NSS had started an investigation into the State Savings Bank, the country's biggest savings institution, after receiving signals that SSB funds were illegally transfered to a private commercial bank.
The service has found a liquidity crisis in another bank as well as irregularities in eight of 28 inspected financial brokerage houses, he added without giving details.
In the past one year Bulgaria's central bank has placed in receivership and sought bankruptcies for 16 or one third of the country's banks after establishing their insolvency.
